title: Kairos: Time-Sensitive Scheduling for Ad-Oriented ML Workloads with Heterogeneous Time-Utility Functions

problem.claim: Ad-oriented ML training tasks have time-sensitive business value that decays when execution is delayed.

gap.claim: Existing schedulers primarily optimize throughput or fairness and lack precise functions for time-dependent business-value decay.

contributions.claim: The paper identifies SLO, softSLO, and BE ad recommendation task types and develops empirically grounded Time-Utility Functions from real-world datasets.
Kairos is a utility-theoretic scheduling algorithm that jointly considers elastic parallelism, heterogeneous deadlines, and time-decaying utilities.
Kairos provides approximation guarantees for SLO and BE tasks under the stated relaxation and approximation conditions.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The Time-Utility Functions are developed using real-world datasets.
Experiments report up to 47% improvement in overall utility preservation compared with state-of-the-art schedulers.

narrative_sequence.summary: Digital advertising uses ML recommendations, whose training tasks have overlooked time-sensitive characteristics.
Recommendation-task value decays rapidly with execution delay, while existing schedulers do not model this decay precisely.
The paper defines three task types and develops Time-Utility Functions from real-world data.
Kairos schedules workloads by reasoning jointly about parallelism, deadlines, and decaying utility.
The abstract reports approximation guarantees and experimental utility-preservation gains.

source_observation.claim: Schedulers that optimize only system-level metrics may fail to preserve task value when workload utility changes over time.

interpretation.claim: Scheduling objectives can incorporate explicit time-dependent utility functions in addition to conventional resource metrics.

application.claim: For time-sensitive ML workloads, classify task value-decay patterns and use them to inform scheduling decisions.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that this approach applies unchanged to workloads without comparable time-dependent business utility.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, workload scale, or experimental configurations.
The abstract does not identify the compared schedulers or report results beyond the maximum 47% improvement.
The abstract does not provide details of the approximation-proof conditions.
